ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The participants are persona agents generated using Claude's Haiku-4.5 model.
Among these five cases, the composition of the focus groups and the availability of information about the participants were compared.
This combination was useful for the simulation because the participants were linked not only to transcripts but also to individual metadata derived from the preliminary survey.

The agents were therefore most consistent about a theme on which the human participants were not, and least consistent about one on which they were. themes are shown along the left, colour coded by category.

Finally, synthetic participants were more linguistically similar to one another and substantially harder to identify or differentiate from each other using their responses, compared to human participants with no clear improvement from profile enrichment.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> The participants are persona agents generated using Claude's Haiku-4.5 model.

> Among these five cases, the composition of the focus groups and the availability of information about the participants were compared.

> This combination was useful for the simulation because the participants were linked not only to transcripts but also to individual metadata derived from the preliminary survey.

> The agents were therefore most consistent about a theme on which the human participants were not, and least consistent about one on which they were. themes are shown along the left, colour coded by category.

> Finally, synthetic participants were more linguistically similar to one another and substantially harder to identify or differentiate from each other using their responses, compared to human participants with no clear improvement from profile enrichment.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found no imprecise *p* values or *p*-values of exactly zero out of 3 detected.

table.formatted: A permutation test confirmed this decisively exceeded chance (p < .001), and all five human sessions were individually above chance.
table.expanded: A permutation test confirmed this decisively exceeded chance (p < .001), and all five human sessions were individually above chance.
The enriched condition performed no better than guessing with 32.5% against its own chance level of 31.2% (p = .34), and its sessions fell on either side of chance in equal measure.

The basic condition barely exceeded chance, 37.7% hits against a chance level of 30.9% (p = .01), although the result was not corroborated when each session was treated as a single observation rather than pooling individual attributions across sessions.

stat_p_exact.report: We found no imprecise *p* values or *p*-values of exactly zero out of 3 detected.

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: The enriched condition performed no better than guessing with 32.5% against its own chance level of 31.2% (p = .34), and its sessions fell on either side of chance in equal measure.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .34", Sentence = "The enriched condition performed no better than guessing with 32.5% against its own chance level of 31.2% (p = .34), and its sessions fell on either side of chance in equal measure."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1595 columns across 148 data files.
#### Issues Identified

273 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 148 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: The participants are persona agents generated using Claude's Haiku-4.5 model.
Among these five cases, the composition of the focus groups and the availability of information about the participants were compared.
This combination was useful for the simulation because the participants were linked not only to transcripts but also to individual metadata derived from the preliminary survey.

The agents were therefore most consistent about a theme on which the human participants were not, and least consistent about one on which they were. themes are shown along the left, colour coded by category.

Finally, synthetic participants were more linguistically similar to one another and substantially harder to identify or differentiate from each other using their responses, compared to human participants with no clear improvement from profile enrichment.

BLINDED_CROSS_MODEL_LLM_ADJUDICATION — frozen protocol for U01-U07 / Q3.

NOT human validation. NOT a neutral judge. NOT ground truth.
It is a second model's opinion, collected under blinding, and it never converts a
human-anchored result into a validated one.

BLINDING
--------
The auditor never sees: the name of the model that produced the candidate themes; the
enriched / demographics-only / human condition; whether a transcript is synthetic or
human; any aggregate result; the 0.6364 benchmark; the B+ state; or the researcher's
view of overall quality. Unit ids are replaced by opaque blinded labels.

It sees only: a blinded unit id, the unit's full text, the reference theme and its
evidence (where the task has one), the candidate theme and ALL of its evidence, and the
frozen rubric for one task.

The two sides are labelled REFERENCE and CANDIDATE — never "human" and "machine" — so
provenance is not recoverable from the prompt.

FOUR SEPARATE TASKS, NEVER ONE HOLISTIC SCORE
---------------------------------------------
  A PAIRWISE_CORRESPONDENCE      does the candidate express the reference's claim
  B MACHINE_THEME_GROUNDEDNESS   is the candidate supported by the unit's own speech
  C MACHINE_ONLY_STATUS          is an unmatched candidate novel, duplicate, or unsupported
  D GRANULARITY                  is a one-to-many / many-to-one a grain difference

Each judgement returns a category, an ordinal confidence, exact quotes, brief reasoning,
and what information would be needed to decide definitively.

ROBUSTNESS
----------
Every case runs TWICE, independently, with the alternatives rotated and distinct cache
keys per repetition_index. Labels are never averaged. A judgement is
CROSS_MODEL_CORROBORATED only if both repetitions agree, both cite valid evidence, the
verdict does not contradict the human substantive-correspondence rule, and confidence is
not LOW. Otherwise CROSS_MODEL_UNRESOLVED.

Researcher-facing matching workbook for the Q3 emergent calibration (V2), plus its gate.

WHY V1 WAS REPLACED
-------------------
Emergent_Matching_Q3_POPULATED.xlsx listed 74 rows with `relation` and `decision` but no
counterpart-key column, so a match could not be expressed at all. The one-sided 44-row
design fixed that. Direct validation of V1 then found three further defects, all fixed
here:

  1. EVIDENCE WAS TRUNCATED. Quotes were cut at 180/200 characters, mid-sentence. The
     researcher was being asked to judge a match against evidence she could not fully
     read. All slicing is gone; every quote is complete. Excel allows 32,767 characters
     per cell, every cell is checked against that before writing, and if any ever
     exceeded it the evidence would move to a one-row-per-quote sheet with an explicit
     reference — never a silent truncation.
  2. IMMUTABLE COLUMNS WERE UNSEALED. Sheet protection is a convenience that any writer
     can switch off. The gate now rebuilds the canonical representation from
     human_reference_q3.json and extraction_results_q3.json and compares every immutable
     cell, including the relation_derived formulas, rejecting any edit, deletion,
     addition or reordering.
  3. UNCERTAIN WAS TREATED AS A MATCH. Keys named on an UNCERTAIN row were flowing into
     the same link set as MATCHED. They are now kept strictly apart: they never count as
     matches, never raise recall, never clear a theme from the adjudication queue, and
     never produce confirmed fusion or fragmentation. While any remain, the overall state
     is UNRESOLVED.

a cross-model adjudicator of the ambiguous cases only. Cross-model consensus is NOT human
validation and is never described as such.

--------------------------------
Not the condition, corpus, focus group or replicate; not Stage B's decision; not Stage

codebook; not any prior result. It sees the theme and the frozen taxonomy, nothing else.

repetitions, so a decision that depended on position would show up as instability

text.text: Objective: the growing commercial use of large language model (LLM)-based synthetic participants raises questions about their validity.
This study evaluates how reliably textbased synthetic focus groups reproduce human thematic content and interactional dynamics.

Methods: the assessment used a matched dataset on animal product consumption and gender to generate 30 text-based synthetic focus-group sessions by manipulating agents' profile levels (basic vs. enriched).
Their transcripts were compared with those of five human focus groups using a novel three-level benchmark: thematic fidelity, interaction process, and speaker distinctiveness.

Results: synthetic groups recovered a plausible subset of human themes but displayed excessive verbosity, internally resolved contrast, less contextually detailed discourse, and reduced speaker distinctiveness.
Profile enrichment increased thematic coverage but concentrated discussions around shared ideas.
Conclusions: these findings position synthetic focus groups as a promising tool for exploratory market research, while underscoring their limitations in capturing situated social interaction.
Their suitability depends on the intended use, requiring multidimensional validation before application.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have triggered a significant debate about their potential use as proxies for human participants in social, psychological, and market research (Sarstedt et al., 2024). Tissaoui (2026) situates this possibility within simulator theory, according to which LLMs can generate contextdependent simulations from statistical regularities learned through large-scale exposure to human language.
text.formatted: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have triggered a significant debate about their potential use as proxies for human participants in social, psychological, and market research <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Sarstedt et al., 2024)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Tissaoui (2026)</ref> situates this possibility within simulator theory, according to which LLMs can generate contextdependent simulations from statistical regularities learned through large-scale exposure to human language.

text.text: From this perspective, persona agents are not fixed psychological entities, but prompt-based constructs that approximate linguistic styles, social roles, and behavioural patterns under specific conditions.
Their possible use as research proxies therefore raises a central theoretical problem: what should count as sufficiently humanlike behaviour for empirical research purposes?

To navigate this challenge, researchers have increasingly opted for pragmatic evaluations, including social science Turing tests or direct replication of human study results, even though the sufficiency of these methods and measures for declaring human-like cognition remains the subject of intense academic debate (Amirova et al., 2024).
text.formatted: To navigate this challenge, researchers have increasingly opted for pragmatic evaluations, including social science Turing tests or direct replication of human study results, even though the sufficiency of these methods and measures for declaring human-like cognition remains the subject of intense academic debate <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amirova et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the concept of algorithmic fidelity has been proposed to describe the extent to which a model's responses can accurately reflect human ideas, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviours within specific sociocultural contexts (Amirova et al., 2024; Argyle et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Thus, the concept of algorithmic fidelity has been proposed to describe the extent to which a model's responses can accurately reflect human ideas, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviours within specific sociocultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amirova et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Argyle et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This drive for innovation stems largely from efficiency pressures both in academic and commercial research, since traditional data collection is by its nature, slow, resource-intensive, and limited by logistical obstacles (Anthis et al., 2025; Toubia et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This drive for innovation stems largely from efficiency pressures both in academic and commercial research, since traditional data collection is by its nature, slow, resource-intensive, and limited by logistical obstacles <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anthis et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Toubia et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For researchers, synthetic participants could lower financial barriers and make larger empirical studies more accessible to underfunded institutions (Sarstedt et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For researchers, synthetic participants could lower financial barriers and make larger empirical studies more accessible to underfunded institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Sarstedt et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In commercial research, they are often expected to accelerate early concept testing, model consumer hypotheses, and simulate hard-to-reach or vulnerable segments before fieldwork (Market Research Society, 2024; Toubia et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In commercial research, they are often expected to accelerate early concept testing, model consumer hypotheses, and simulate hard-to-reach or vulnerable segments before fieldwork <ref type="bibr">(Market Research Society, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Toubia et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, this enthusiasm introduces a tension, as the desire for rapid, cost-effective scaling risks overlooking unresolved questions about the cognitive coherence and validity of these simulated selves (Tissaoui, 2026).
text.formatted: However, this enthusiasm introduces a tension, as the desire for rapid, cost-effective scaling risks overlooking unresolved questions about the cognitive coherence and validity of these simulated selves <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tissaoui, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The deployment of persona agents is no longer a speculative idea, as large-scale databases containing individuals' data are already being developed to support empirical research in automated surveys, deep interviews, opinion prediction models, and synthetic focus groups.

For instance, NVIDIA has released the Nemotron-Personas collection, a set of multilingual, region-specific synthetic person datasets that currently covers seven countries, and approximately 53 million synthetic people, each based on real-world demographic and geographic distributions (Meyer & Corneil, 2026).
text.formatted: For instance, NVIDIA has released the Nemotron-Personas collection, a set of multilingual, region-specific synthetic person datasets that currently covers seven countries, and approximately 53 million synthetic people, each based on real-world demographic and geographic distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Meyer & Corneil, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In parallel, the Twin-2K-500 dataset is a large-scale public repository containing detailed behavioural, demographic, and psychological profiles of over 2,000 people in the United States (US), designed specifically to ground, train, and validate LLM digital twin simulations through a comprehensive battery of over 500 questions across different domains (Toubia et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In parallel, the Twin-2K-500 dataset is a large-scale public repository containing detailed behavioural, demographic, and psychological profiles of over 2,000 people in the United States (US), designed specifically to ground, train, and validate LLM digital twin simulations through a comprehensive battery of over 500 questions across different domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Toubia et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these large-scale deployments demonstrate that the creation of synthetic populations is an increasingly established technical practice already integrated into research workflows.
However, many of these applications remain part of internal industry processes, leaving their methods poorly documented and difficult to evaluate through independent academic scrutiny.

The scale of these implementations may suggest that they were developed primarily with quantitative applications in mind, which appear to dominate the current literature and often rely on large volumes of data.
Synthetic focus groups, in contrast, present a more demanding validation problem by shifting the target from isolated output plausibility to sustained multi-agent interaction (Amirova et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Synthetic focus groups, in contrast, present a more demanding validation problem by shifting the target from isolated output plausibility to sustained multi-agent interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amirova et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although generating dialogue may appear well suited to LLMs, conversational fluency alone does not demonstrate the reasoning or social understanding required in focus groups (Jones et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although generating dialogue may appear well suited to LLMs, conversational fluency alone does not demonstrate the reasoning or social understanding required in focus groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Jones et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Wen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Focus groups' insights emerge through participants responding to, contesting, and developing one another's contributions rather than through isolated answers (Lim, 2025; Stewart & Shamdasani, 2014).
text.formatted: Focus groups' insights emerge through participants responding to, contesting, and developing one another's contributions rather than through isolated answers <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lim, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Stewart & Shamdasani, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Validation must therefore consider whether agents can sustain multi-turn exchanges, respond meaningfully to peers, negotiate disagreement, and preserve contextual continuity (Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Validation must therefore consider whether agents can sustain multi-turn exchanges, respond meaningfully to peers, negotiate disagreement, and preserve contextual continuity <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Liu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Zhang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although synthetic focus groups remain comparatively underexamined in the literature, their potential value for exploratory research, pilot testing, and decision support makes them an important object of study (Anthis et al., 2025; Novelli et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although synthetic focus groups remain comparatively underexamined in the literature, their potential value for exploratory research, pilot testing, and decision support makes them an important object of study <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anthis et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Novelli et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This gap is also difficult to address because evaluation practices are still in the development phase.
There is still no common standard for validating or auditing tools or systems that use synthetic participants (Sarstedt et al., 2024).
text.formatted: There is still no common standard for validating or auditing tools or systems that use synthetic participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Sarstedt et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because these methods are being developed so quickly and examined so unevenly, it remains unclear how stable they really are or how far their claims of human-likeness can be trusted.
Yet, several companies are already selling services of synthetic market research such as Simile, Getminds, Aaru, Artifical Societies, Ditto, Symar and Evidenza (Toubia et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Yet, several companies are already selling services of synthetic market research such as Simile, Getminds, Aaru, Artifical Societies, Ditto, Symar and Evidenza <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Toubia et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Within the literature on LLM-based social simulation, it is crucial to differentiate between task-oriented agents, which are configured to execute workflows, use tools, or achieve defined operational objectives, and persona agents, which are designed to represent people intending to mimic human behaviour and are the focus of this research (Tissaoui, 2026; Simmons & Hare, 2023).
text.formatted: Within the literature on LLM-based social simulation, it is crucial to differentiate between task-oriented agents, which are configured to execute workflows, use tools, or achieve defined operational objectives, and persona agents, which are designed to represent people intending to mimic human behaviour and are the focus of this research <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tissaoui, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmons & Hare, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Depending on their level of empirical grounding, persona agents can be classified as: ungrounded personas (based on generic prompts), synthetic populations (aligned with statistical distributions), or, at the highest level of fidelity, digital twins or digital shadows (computational representations anchored in data from specific individuals) (Novelli et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Depending on their level of empirical grounding, persona agents can be classified as: ungrounded personas (based on generic prompts), synthetic populations (aligned with statistical distributions), or, at the highest level of fidelity, digital twins or digital shadows (computational representations anchored in data from specific individuals) <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Novelli et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These systems are trained using demographic, biographical, and/or psychographic information to predict how a social profile might express itself or interact (Argyle et al., 2023; Du et al., 2025; Park et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These systems are trained using demographic, biographical, and/or psychographic information to predict how a social profile might express itself or interact <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Argyle et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Du et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Park et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Their evaluation therefore cannot be reduced to task efficiency.

The relevant criterion is predicting human ideas, preferences, beliefs, and actions in situated contexts (Amirova et al., 2024; Argyle et al., 2023), without assuming equivalence in the underlying cognitive mechanisms (Lin, 2025).
text.formatted: The relevant criterion is predicting human ideas, preferences, beliefs, and actions in situated contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amirova et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Argyle et al., 2023)</ref>, without assuming equivalence in the underlying cognitive mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In theory, basing persona agents on more information should yield higher fidelity results, however the evidence here is mixed. Park et al. (2024), for instance, collected in-depth interviews from a stratified representative sample of 1,052 US individuals to build highly invested digital twins.
text.formatted: In theory, basing persona agents on more information should yield higher fidelity results, however the evidence here is mixed. <ref type="bibr">Park et al. (2024)</ref>, for instance, collected in-depth interviews from a stratified representative sample of 1,052 US individuals to build highly invested digital twins.

text.text: When provided with complete transcripts of two-hour interviews as the agent's memory, these generative agents predicted General Social Survey responses with 85% of the test-retest stability observed in the human participants when assessed two weeks later.
But when the architecture was simplified to context paragraphs or demographic profiles, the accuracy dropped to 70% and 71%, respectively.

In contrast, Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) demonstrate that progressively enriching personas from basic age-gender profiles to descriptions including education, decision style, and personal background actually reduced individuality of the synthetic personas.
text.formatted: In contrast, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bhattacharyya et al. (2026)</ref> demonstrate that progressively enriching personas from basic age-gender profiles to descriptions including education, decision style, and personal background actually reduced individuality of the synthetic personas.

text.text: Rather than making the agents more distinct, richer profiles brought their embeddings closer together.

These embeddings can be understood as points on a multi-dimensional semantic map the model uses to produce a response, the farther apart the points are, the more differently the model understands each persona.
As further attributes were added, the distance between these points decreased by approximately 23% to 59%, depending on the model and the task.
This contraction also appeared behaviourally, as simple agegender profiles outperformed richer profiles in tasks like predicting email clicks and social-media engagement.

The findings seem to be mostly explained by the unpredictable way models internally interpret or aggregate these profiles in each scenario from their training, where certain attributes help to anchor the persona while others act as mere distractors that confuse the model.
In other words, greater detail in an agent does not necessarily lead to better replicability of behaviour.

Some authors call it "persona manifold collapse" or "focalism", as the phenomenon in which including several attributes can reduce response diversity, homogenise agents, or make particular characteristics disproportionately influential (Bhattacharyya et al., 2026; Toubia et al., 2025; Hu & Collier, 2024).
text.formatted: Some authors call it "persona manifold collapse" or "focalism", as the phenomenon in which including several attributes can reduce response diversity, homogenise agents, or make particular characteristics disproportionately influential <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bhattacharyya et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Toubia et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hu & Collier, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Another weakness of LLMs that must be acknowledged is the "hyper-accuracy distortion," in which synthetic responses may be technically correct but socially implausible for the simulated profile, alongside differences in tone and structure that reduce authenticity (Amirova et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Another weakness of LLMs that must be acknowledged is the "hyper-accuracy distortion," in which synthetic responses may be technically correct but socially implausible for the simulated profile, alongside differences in tone and structure that reduce authenticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amirova et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, in an experimental setting where simulated average human voters were asked to estimate the number of African countries in the UN, 99.4% gave the exact correct answer, a statistical impossibility for a common human sample (Lin, 2025).
text.formatted: For example, in an experimental setting where simulated average human voters were asked to estimate the number of African countries in the UN, 99.4% gave the exact correct answer, a statistical impossibility for a common human sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the presented limitations, the initial findings on synthetic agents are promising enough to warrant further investigation (Anthis et al., 2025), but not strong enough to support definitive claims about their use as a substitute for humans.
text.formatted: Despite the presented limitations, the initial findings on synthetic agents are promising enough to warrant further investigation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anthis et al., 2025)</ref>, but not strong enough to support definitive claims about their use as a substitute for humans.

text.text: In relatively closed tasks, such as surveys and behavioural experiments, LLM agents appear to approximate aggregate human patterns under specific prompting and contextualization conditions.

As an illustrative example of predicting behaviour in unprecedented situations, Kozlowski and colleagues (2024) used GPT-3 (a model trained on data cut off in October 2019) to simulate political polarization in the US in the face of COVID-19.
text.formatted: As an illustrative example of predicting behaviour in unprecedented situations, <ref type="bibr">Kozlowski and colleagues (2024)</ref> used GPT-3 (a model trained on data cut off in October 2019) to simulate political polarization in the US in the face of COVID-19.

text.text: After configuring the agents as strongly partisan Republicans or Democrats, they evaluated their positions and justifications regarding 49 unique issues related to the pandemic.

By comparing the results with actual 2020 surveys, using individual regression models and complementary tests, they found that in 84% of cases, the agents reflected the same public divisions on vaccines, masks, and business closures.
Furthermore, their justifications mirrored actual partisan reasoning, with conservatives appealing to personal freedom and liberals to public safety.

Although this study leaves open the question of to what extent less polarized profiles are replicated, it indicates that agents can use an ideological profile to closely predict complex social dynamics, making them a very promising tool for exploratory research.
Regarding evidence from focus groups studies, the results are fragmented because the literature has approached these simulations analytically in different ways.

Some studies focus solely on the content produced by the focus groups while others additionally consider the interactions. Zhang et al. (2024) compared five human sessions involving 23 participants against simulated groups that were grounded in one-minute personal introductions.
text.formatted: Some studies focus solely on the content produced by the focus groups while others additionally consider the interactions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Zhang et al. (2024)</ref> compared five human sessions involving 23 participants against simulated groups that were grounded in one-minute personal introductions.

text.text: These introductions provided demographics, screen-time usage (the core topic of the focus group), and a distinctive "voice print".
As a result, the human transcripts yielded 39 specific codes, defined as descriptive unique tags that summarize ideas raised in the discussion, which were grouped into four broad themes.
The synthetic agents, in contrast, produced 47 codes grouped into five themes.
Notably, the simulated groups successfully replicated 87% of human codes demonstrating high capture, while the AI introduced 13 entirely new codes and a fifth broad theme.
The analysis suggests a positive broad thematic coverage nuanced by the fact that synthetic agents included ideas that real participants never actually brought up.

The researchers did not assess in depth how agents arrived at that result, making only a brief statement that humans, unlike synths, "build upon previous contributions and enrich discussions with personal experiences" (Zhang et al., 2024, p. 7). text.text: They found that both groups successfully completed the discussion guide and provided responses relevant to the topic of discussion.
However, the artificial participants exhibited a severe lack of diversity, as the synthetic agents agreed with one another 92% of the time, compared to only a 42% agreement rate among real humans.
The researchers also noticed a clear lack of natural flow in the agents' responses.

Unlike humans, who often deviate from the topic or give brief replies averaging just 92 words, the agents addressed every part of the question with rigid and formal responses, averaging a much longer 195 words.
In other words, interactions within the synthetic focus groups were unlike those seen in human focus groups.

For this reason, the limited studies that directly examine synthetic focus groups should not be treated as separate benchmarks, but as partial views that need to be integrated into a benchmark able to assess both thematic and interactional fidelity.
The next section therefore turns specifically to focus groups, examining their methodological value and the particular demands they place on synthetic social simulation.
In qualitative research, focus groups are a central technique for studying social, cultural, and consumer phenomena.

Their methodological value lies not only in gathering various individual opinions, but also in creating a conversational setting in which participants can respond to one another, clarify their points, challenge each other, adjust or reinforce ideas and preferences, and collaboratively construct meaning in real time (Nyumba et al., 2018; Stewart & Shamdasani, 2014; Lunt & Livingstone, 1996).

text.text: This discussion of qualitative quality connects with empirical evidence on data saturation, particularly regarding sample size.
In a study of 40 focus groups, Guest et al. (2017) found that more than 80% of themes appeared in the first two or three groups, while 90% emerged between three and six sessions.
text.formatted: In a study of 40 focus groups, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Guest et al. (2017)</ref> found that more than 80% of themes appeared in the first two or three groups, while 90% emerged between three and six sessions.

text.text: Three groups were also sufficient to identify the most prevalent themes in the dataset.
To ensure that group size did not skew these findings the researchers intentionally kept all sessions consistent at six to eight participants.

Similarly, Hennink et al. (2019) distinguish between code saturation (the point when no new topics emerge from the data) and meaning saturation (when researchers consider they fully understand all the details and nuances of the raised topics) based on an empirical evaluation of 10 focus groups.

(2019)</ref> distinguish between code saturation (the point when no new topics emerge from the data) and meaning saturation (when researchers consider they fully understand all the details and nuances of the raised topics) based on an empirical evaluation of 10 focus groups.

text.text: In their analysis, four focus groups were sufficient for code saturation, although meaning saturation required additional sessions, especially when designs included different participant sub-groups such as age or gender.
These findings align with broader methodological consensus.
In a subsequent systematic review of 23 articles assessing saturation, Hennink and Kaiser (2022) identified six empirical studies that tested focus group saturation.
text.formatted: In a subsequent systematic review of 23 articles assessing saturation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hennink and Kaiser (2022)</ref> identified six empirical studies that tested focus group saturation.

text.text: Their review concluded that saturation is typically reached within a narrow range of four to eight sessions.
However, the quality of discussion remains harder to define in operational terms.

According to the above, focus group quality appears to be mainly driven by subjectively judging the relevance and depth of the information produced regarding the research objective rather than relying on standardized indicators.

Theory highlights some expected behaviours, such as balanced participation, whether participant responses contain concrete details (specific times, places, actions, people, or decisions) rather than generic opinion, moderator questions don't imply a "correct" answer, or completeness of the planned discussion guide (Acocella & Cataldi, 2021; Nyumba et al., 2018).

text.text: In summary, focus group outputs can be assessed on at least three levels: the
For this study, a custom system was developed to generate synthetic focus groups, in order to maintain control and traceability over the elements that make up the simulation.

The architecture allows persona agents to converse following real discussion guides presented by a moderator agent within a structure that approximates some basic features of focus group dynamics, including speaking turns not being predefined and the moderator being able to adapt the guide according to the flow of the discussion.
Its ultimate function was to produce focus groups in text form and generate synthetic transcripts comparable to human ones.
The system is organized into three main roles: participants, moderator, and orchestrator (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: The system is organized into three main roles: participants, moderator, and orchestrator (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: The participants are persona agents generated using Claude's Haiku-4.5 model.
Each persona agent corresponds to a specific participant in the original human focus group and is constructed from the participant-level information available for that person in the source dataset.
The selected information is stored in an individual JSON file, which serves as a structured participant profile, allowing all agents to be created using the same format.
Just before an agent intervenes, the system converts this profile into a natural-language description so that the model can respond based on that profile.
For example, one of the participants might be presented to the model as follows: "You are John, a 33-year-old male participant in a focus group.
You live in an urban area in Scotland, UK.
Your typical eating patterns -speak from these naturally; do not list them, just let them inform your answers -include: red meat once a week..."
The moderator, generated using Claude's Sonnet-4.6 model, leads the session by following the discussion guide, but without mechanically repeating it.
At each turn, the moderator first decides whether to intervene or let the conversation continue among the participants.
If the moderator intervenes, they can choose from actions such as delving deeper into a topic, addressing a specific participant, or moving on to the next section.
This decision is made within a set of actions defined in the system (see Appendix B), although the content of each intervention is generated by the model.

That set of actions is based on the functions that the literature attributes to a human moderator: clarifying and regulating the discussion, supporting the generation of information, and facilitating interaction (Acocella & Cataldi, 2021).
text.formatted: That set of actions is based on the functions that the literature attributes to a human moderator: clarifying and regulating the discussion, supporting the generation of information, and facilitating interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Acocella & Cataldi, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, the orchestrator is not an agent, nor does it make its own calls to the model; rather, it is an internal layer of code.

Its function is to handle the administrative aspects of the session so that the moderator can focus on leading the discussion, while the orchestrator maintains the operational continuity of the session.

Specifically, the orchestrator compiles the transcript from the moderator's and participants' contributions, keeps track of speaking turns, records basic participation metrics, and uses that information to apply a fixed-rule algorithm to determine which participant speaks next.
Participants (a set of persona agents participating in the focus group), and the Orchestrator (software to coordinate and record the interactions).
Beyond this general architecture, it is worth clarifying how memory operates within a session, since it shapes what each agent can plausibly respond to.
Participant agents do not have a separate memory store or private notes about the discussion.
When called to speak, each participant receives its own prior response history together with the conversation that has occurred since it last spoke, rendered as plain transcript text.
In this sense, the participant's "memory" is not an independent record of the session, but the conversational context that is reintroduced at each turn.
The moderator has a different memory structure.
It keeps a small set of running notes, updated after most turns.
These notes track themes that have appeared, possible contradictions in participants' earlier statements, and whether the group is moving too quickly toward smooth consensus.
The moderator's access to the transcript also depends on the structure of the discussion guide.
Each guide section is treated as an active discussion block, defined by a main question and its sub-questions.
While that block remains open, the moderator can see the full transcript of everything said within it, allowing it to decide whether to probe further, redirect the discussion, or move on.
When the system advances to the next section, the previous block is compressed into a short summary.
From that point onward, the moderator no longer rereads the full transcript of the closed section, but relies on this summary as part of its memory of earlier discussion.
The participation algorithm seeks to operationalize the way in which turns can emerge in a group discussion.

As illustrated in Figure 2, instead of assigning a fixed order, the system conducts an "auction" of turns: in each round, each participant privately evaluates (via their own API call) whether they want to speak based on the current context of the discussion (last 6 transcript entries) and assigns an urgency value between 0 and 1.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>, instead of assigning a fixed order, the system conducts an "auction" of turns: in each round, each participant privately evaluates (via their own API call) whether they want to speak based on the current context of the discussion (last 6 transcript entries) and assigns an urgency value between 0 and 1.

text.text: To enter the auction, a participant must want to intervene and exceed the threshold of 0.55.
If several participants exceed this threshold, the orchestrator selects the one with the highest urgency, with the tiebreaker favouring the agent who has spoken the least.
The auction is modified to capture dynamics typical of a focus group.
If someone is named by another participant, or if the moderator directs a question to several members, that person receives a limited bonus.
However, if the moderator names a single participant, there is no auction: that person responds directly, simulating the moment when the group's attention shifts to the person who was addressed.

Furthermore, if there is a high level of consensus, the system slightly favours those who wish to challenge the group; and if six turns pass without the moderator intervening, the system returns control to the moderator.
The starting point was the identification of datasets from human focus groups that could serve as a basis for comparison.
After searching open repositories, 15 studies were identified.
Of these, only five had discussion guides and verbatim transcripts available.
Among these five cases, the composition of the focus groups and the availability of information about the participants were compared.
Based on this review, Macho Meals (Hankins et al., 2025) was selected as the main case study, as it was the dataset that offered the greatest detail for constructing persona agents.
text.formatted: Based on this review, Macho Meals <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hankins et al., 2025)</ref> was selected as the main case study, as it was the dataset that offered the greatest detail for constructing persona agents.

text.text: It was decided to work with data linked to previously published studies not only because they had been collected by external researchers but also because they were accompanied by a prior analysis and findings that had been peer-reviewed as part of the academic publication process.
This provided an initial reference regarding the expected themes and patterns in human groups, without that reference depending on the design of the present synthetic system.
Using the Macho Meals dataset (Hankins et al., 2025), a set of 22 persona agents was developed, corresponding to the male participants in the five focus groups from the original study.
text.formatted: Using the Macho Meals dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hankins et al., 2025)</ref>, a set of 22 persona agents was developed, corresponding to the male participants in the five focus groups from the original study.

text.text: The participants ranged in age from 20 to 73 years, with a mean age of 43.1 years (SD = 15.8).

This study, conducted in the UK, examined the relationship between the consumption of animal products and masculinity through a first quantitative phase and a second qualitative phase involving remotely moderated focus groups.
This combination was useful for the simulation because the participants were linked not only to transcripts but also to individual metadata derived from the preliminary survey.

For each participant, the following were recorded: pseudonym, age, gender, region, type of region, diet, scales related to masculinity and meat consumption, and frequency of consumption of red meat, chicken, fish, eggs, and dairy products.
These data were used to construct the profiles without adding unobserved biographical details.
The study employs a comparative focus group simulation design with experimental manipulation of the anchor level in the agents' profiles.
To this end, the five Macho Meals focus groups were simulated three times each, maintaining the same participant composition as in the human reference group.
These repetitions aim to mitigate the stochasticity inherent in LLM models, given that the inability to set a seed generates variability in responses to the same stimulus (Larooij & Törnberg, 2025).
text.formatted: These repetitions aim to mitigate the stochasticity inherent in LLM models, given that the inability to set a seed generates variability in responses to the same stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Larooij & Törnberg, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: All sessions followed the original study's protocol, consisting of an introduction, five questions, and a conclusion.
The analysis contrasts two conditions.
In the basic condition, the agents are configured exclusively with demographic data.

In the enriched condition, the agents incorporate all available metadata from the original study, which includes demographic information, dietary habits, and psychographic variables related to masculinity and meat consumption.
This design allowed us to evaluate whether less detailed profiles can replicate human behaviour patterns with algorithmic fidelity equivalent to that of the more comprehensive profiles.
Accordingly, the study generated 30 synthetic focus-group sessions (5 focus groups × 2 conditions × 3 replications), alongside the five human sessions used as references (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: Accordingly, the study generated 30 synthetic focus-group sessions (5 focus groups × 2 conditions × 3 replications), alongside the five human sessions used as references (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>).

text.text: The median execution time was 23.3 minutes per synthetic session, ranging from 13.1 to 42.2 minutes.
The median cost was USD 2.54 per synth session, with individual sessions costing between USD 1.39 and USD 3.98, for a total cost of USD 75.38 across all 30 synthetic sessions.

The evaluation benchmark consisted of 12 indicators, organized into three levels, designed to determine the extent to which synthetic focus groups replicate the properties of the human focus groups used as a reference.

Given that focus group data are constructed in a situated and collective manner, the evaluation does not seek to verify whether the synthetic data meet a predefined quality standard, but rather to contrast them with human data: each indicator expresses a gap between the two, and it is the human transcripts that set the benchmark.

The indicators were based on the differences documented in the literature between synthetic and human participants, for example, greater verbosity, homogenization of voices, less dissent, the moderator's prominence, or lower specificity, and by incorporating findings from previous studies on synthetic focus groups and the evaluation of persona agents (e.g. Zhang et al. (2024  2024)).
text.formatted: The indicators were based on the differences documented in the literature between synthetic and human participants, for example, greater verbosity, homogenization of voices, less dissent, the moderator's prominence, or lower specificity, and by incorporating findings from previous studies on synthetic focus groups and the evaluation of persona agents (e.g. <ref type="formula">Zhang et al. (2024</ref>  <ref type="formula">2024)</ref>).

text.text: It should be noted that the comparison was always made at the group, not participant, level.

Although each human group had only one transcript, the five transcripts taken together show the extent to which the groups differ, and, when a metric allows for it, that variation becomes the criterion for evaluating the distance between a synthetic group and its human counterpart.
Comparing each simulation with its own group and presenting the results group by group takes this limitation into account without eliminating it.

The first level, thematic fidelity, uses the codebook designed by the researchers in the original study (see Figure 4): a structured set of codes (labels of categories and themes with their definitions) that serves as a framework for classifying the content of the transcripts.
text.formatted: The first level, thematic fidelity, uses the codebook designed by the researchers in the original study (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">4</ref>): a structured set of codes (labels of categories and themes with their definitions) that serves as a framework for classifying the content of the transcripts.

text.text: Coding is performed by an evaluator LLM from a different family than the generator, blindly and identically on both sides, to avoid circularity between the evaluator (Gemini) and the generator (Claude).
Before being used, the evaluator LLM must pass three quality control checks.

Reproducibility checked whether the evaluator coded the same transcript identically across multiple iterations, to ensure that any differences observed between human and synthetic groups do not stem from variability within the LLM itself.

Discrimination verified whether each human transcript achieves greater thematic overlap with its paired synthetic version than with synthetics from other groups, ensuring that the metric captures specific similarities rather than just general matches.

Citation validity required that every coding decision be supported by a word-for-word verbatim confirmation in the transcript; any code without verifiable evidence was discarded, reducing the risk of citations fabricated by the LLM (for more detail see Appendix C).
Beyond the first level of thematic fidelity, which focuses on content generation, the benchmark extends to two additional dimensions.

The second level examined how the conversation unfolded, focusing on the length of turns and their distribution, how much that length varied from one focus group to another, the extent to which a turn raised and resolved conflicting positions on its own, and the density with which the discourse was anchored in specific contextual details.

The third level, as a complementary analysis, addressed the distinguishability of speakers, that is, whether participants in the same session can be distinguished from one another and whether any of them maintain a recognizable way of speaking from one question to the next.
Both properties are measured within each session by comparing participants with their own peers, and never by comparing a synthetic participant with the human whose profile was used to construct it.
The resulting values at the group level were then compared across conditions.
For details on each of the indicators, see Appendix D.
The initial analyses were conducted to determine how well the two different groups of synthetic agents (basic vs. enriched) reproduced the themes present in the human data.
The human focus groups produced a total of 11 different themes.
In comparison, both sets of agents reproduced only part of the human repertoire, and the themes they repeated most consistently were not the human ones.
Focus group discussion among the basic synths produced an average of 4.7 themes while the enriched synths covered 5.7 of them on average.
In other words, the synthetic focus groups covered roughly half as many topics as their human counterparts.
The contrast was sharper for consistency.
To illustrate this, Figure 5 maps exactly how many times each theme occurred (out of a maximum of 5) across the baseline and the six synthetic replications (3x basic and 3x enriched).
text.formatted: To illustrate this, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">5</ref> maps exactly how many times each theme occurred (out of a maximum of 5) across the baseline and the six synthetic replications (3x basic and 3x enriched).

text.text: Looking at the human column, two themes were present in all five groups: Nice and Not nice.
The enriched replicates matched only the first, and only in two of the three replications, whereas the replications with basic synths matched neither.
Not nice, the theme most robustly shared across the human groups, reached at most one of the five groups in any synthetic replicate.
Conversely, Does influence was present in all five groups of every synthetic replicate, yet in only three of the five human groups.

The agents were therefore most consistent about a theme on which the human participants were not, and least consistent about one on which they were. themes are shown along the left, colour coded by category.
The first column shows the number of human focus groups (out of 5) that raised each theme.
The next six columns report the number of synthetic focus groups (out of 5) that raised each theme.
The cells' colour ranges from light (0) to dark (5) to visually illustrate the consistency effects.
Turning to theme saturation, Figure 6 tracks how quickly each study condition exhausted its own thematic repertoire.
text.formatted: Turning to theme saturation, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">6</ref> tracks how quickly each study condition exhausted its own thematic repertoire.

text.text: Rather than measuring against the full 11-theme human baseline, this analysis evaluates each replicate against its own final output to identify the exact point when new contributions ceased.
The human baseline followed a common qualitative trajectory, generating most of its themes in the early sessions and reaching a stable levelling off after the third group.

This is consistent with empirical evidence indicating that relatively homogenous human focus groups attached to narrow research objectives typically reach code saturation by the fourth group (Hennink et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This is consistent with empirical evidence indicating that relatively homogenous human focus groups attached to narrow research objectives typically reach code saturation by the fourth group <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hennink et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The synthetic replications, however, diverged significantly from this expected human behaviour, displaying marked instability across runs.
On one extreme, the basic synths occasionally exhibited premature saturation, exhausting its entirely limited repertoire as early as the first session (Basic Replication-2).
On the other extreme, multiple synthetic runs continued to drip-feed single new themes up to the fifth group, failing to demonstrate a consistent levelling off at all.

This erratic pattern demonstrates that while synthetic agents do accumulate themes, they fail to replicate the natural convergence and stabilization characteristic of human focus groups. saturation point is the last focus group that added a new codebook theme.
"Not observed" indications that FG5 still added themes so no stable plateau was reached.
Shifting the focus away from complete replications, it is equally important to measure how accurately the models replicated specific, isolated conversations.
To do this, we averaged the three synthetic runs for a given focus group, compared them to their direct human counterpart, and used three specific metrics.
Recall captured the percentage of themes from a specific human group that its synthetic counterpart successfully managed to elicit.
Precision looked at the other side of the equation, indicating how many of the themes generated by a synthetic group actually matched its specific human baseline.
Finally, reach measured how widely a theme spread among the participants.
For any theme that actually came up during a session, reach calculates the average percentage of participants who explicitly mentioned it, backed by a verified quote.
To illustrate these dynamics, Figure 7 plots the performance across all five sessions.
text.formatted: To illustrate these dynamics, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">7</ref> plots the performance across all five sessions.

text.text: In this graph, large markers represent the mean performance for a given condition, while the small open markers display the three individual runs, highlighting the natural variance in the models' outputs.
When looking at the group-by-group averages (e.g.
FG1 human vs.
FG1 enriched), the enriched synths achieved a mean recall of 39.1%, while the basic synths trailed at 27.0%.
Precision, however, remained strong across the board.
The enriched groups saw 78.8% of their produced themes match the human data, and the basic groups reached 71.0%.
What these values suggest is that while the simulations generated a narrower range of themes than the human baseline, the content they did manage to produce was largely accurate.
The differences between the conditions became much more pronounced when examining reach.
In the enriched sessions, a given theme was expressed by an average of 77.1% of the participants.
This represents an increase over both the human baseline (58.9%) and the basic sessions (65.4%).
In other words, enriching the profiles pushed the synthetic participants to cluster more tightly around a shared set of themes.
Notably, 44.6% of the enriched themes were voiced by every single group member.
To put this in perspective, that level of full-group consensus only occurred for 14.9% of the themes in the human groups and 23.3% in the basic groups.
In other words, the synth focus group discussions looked less like real people.
They overstated how widely any given view was shared and lost the minority views and disagreement that real groups contained.
Large markers show the mean of the three runs.
Small markers show individual runs (R1-3).
In the reach panel, diamonds show the paired human reference for each focus group.
The greatest differences between human and synthetic groups occurred not in their thematic content, but in how the conversations actually unfolded.
The most noticeable divergence was verbosity.

Because turn lengths were strongly right-skewed, with a few exceptionally long interventions pulling up the arithmetic mean, central tendency was calculated as the median within each session and then averaged across sessions, giving each session equal weight.

On average, human participant turns (from when a participant began speaking until they finished or were interrupted) were concise: 43% contained 40 words or fewer and 41% ranged from 41 to 150 words, with a per-group median turn length averaging 49 words.
To illustrate how these proportions compare across conditions, Figure 8 displays the full distribution of participant turn lengths.
text.formatted: To illustrate how these proportions compare across conditions, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">8</ref> displays the full distribution of participant turn lengths.

text.text: The simulations generated considerably longer responses, with 93% (basic) and 90% (enriched) of their turns spanning 151 to 400 words and group medians of roughly 240 words.
The contrast is clearest among the shortest turns, with 34% of human turns falling below 25 words, whereas the shortest synthetic turn in the entire corpus of thirty sessions was 55 words.

Moreover, human groups varied widely, with focus group medians ranging from 22 to 90 words with a coefficient of variation (CV, the percentage that the standard deviation represents relative to the mean) of 51.0%.
In contrast, the synthetic conditions displayed uniformity across sessions since the equivalent between-group CV was 5.6% in the enriched condition and 6.6% in the basic condition.
This shows that whereas human groups developed distinct conversational rhythms per group, the simulations applied a uniform output style regardless of group identity.
That spread also puts the size of the gap in perspective.
The largest difference between any two human focus groups is 68 words, and every one of the 30 synthetic sessions is further than that from its own human counterpart.
It was not possible to reliably determine the differences in the degree of consensus among participants of the different conditions.
As exemplified in Figure 9, synthetic responses frequently combined acknowledgement, counterpoint and balance within a single turn.
text.formatted: As exemplified in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">9</ref>, synthetic responses frequently combined acknowledgement, counterpoint and balance within a single turn.

text.text: The pattern was first noticed while labelling the Level 1 analysis, and was then measured across all 779 participant-to-participant response mentions with a fixed list of contrastive expressions, resulting in 9.8% of synthetic mentions setting out two or more contrasting positions within the same turn, against 0.3% of human mentions.

Rather than presenting a brief idea for another participant to challenge or build upon, the AI agents tended to anticipate alternative perspectives and resolve them internally before finishing the turn.
Finally, to measure response specificity, references such as times, places, people, or food were counted.
Because synthetic agents repeatedly name-dropped their assigned profiles (like London or Birmingham), geographic origins were excluded across all conditions.
After this correction, human turns maintained a higher overall density of contextual references (3.17 per 100 words) than the basic (1.27) and enriched conditions (1.67), as shown in Figure 10.

The sharpest gap appeared in references most closely related to the research topic of macho meals, named foods or dishes, where humans averaged 2.02 references per 100 words, compared to 0.89 in the enriched groups and just 0.24 in the basic groups. maximum across the five focus groups.
The human data are the observed counts whereas the values for the Enriched and Basic groups are the mean over their three replications.
This final level evaluated whether participants maintained unique, recognizable identities rather than blending into a single generic voice.

To test this, two complementary methods were applied to standardized-length text fragments extracted from identical questions across sessions: a predictive attribution test and a descriptive similarity measure.

First, an algorithm built a linguistic profile for each participant using a subset of questions and then tested whether it could correctly attribute an unseen fragment from a different question back to the correct individual.
In the human groups, the task succeeded on 46.8% of attributions, against the 25.5% that random guessing would yield given the number of candidate speakers in each test.
A permutation test confirmed this decisively exceeded chance (p < .001), and all five human sessions were individually above chance.
text.formatted: A permutation test confirmed this decisively exceeded chance (p < .001), and all five human sessions were individually above chance.

text.text: The enriched condition performed no better than guessing with 32.5% against its own chance level of 31.2% (p = .34), and its sessions fell on either side of chance in equal measure.

The basic condition barely exceeded chance, 37.7% hits against a chance level of 30.9% (p = .01), although the result was not corroborated when each session was treated as a single observation rather than pooling individual attributions across sessions.
Second, lexical similarity measured how far two participants' wording overlapped when both were answering the same focus group question.
Comparing them on the same question holds the topic constant so what remains is how each person expresses their answer.
Scores run from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical).
The medians were 0.179 in the human groups, 0.258 in the basic condition and 0.268 in the enriched one.
Synthetic participants resembled one another roughly 45 to 50 per cent more than human participants did.
The two analyses therefore converged: synthetic voices were less distinguishable and more homogeneous, with no clear advantage from enrichment.
This study provides a new benchmark to evaluate the fidelity of LLM-generated focus groups, mapping how well they replicate both the thematic content and the interactive dynamics of human discourse.

Rather than seeking a binary verdict on whether synthetic focus groups are 'faithful' to human counterparts, this research evaluates them across three distinct levels of performance to identify where simulations approximate human behaviour and where they diverge.
The results reveal that human-likeness depends both on the dimension being assessed and the research's intended use of synthetic focus groups.
The synthetic focus groups tested captured a smaller, although largely plausible, set of the human themes raised in the conversation, and the enriched profiles improved this capture.

Nevertheless, while synthetic groups reproduced the substantive content of the discourse with some success, they did so with lower thematic consistency and missed subtle nuances, differing significantly in how participants socially structured their interactions, thus highlighting a core asymmetry between content fidelity and interactive organization This distinction is important because an incomplete thematic reconstruction does not necessarily invalidate the use of synthetic focus groups.

For exploratory applications, such as testing a discussion guide, identifying candidate questions for further studies or anticipating possible lines of response, recovering a plausible subset of human themes may be sufficient.

This interpretation is consistent with Novelli et al. (2026), who distinguish between instrumental uses of simulation and those in which interaction and the collective construction of meaning constitute the central object of interest.
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Novelli et al. (2026)</ref>, who distinguish between instrumental uses of simulation and those in which interaction and the collective construction of meaning constitute the central object of interest.

text.text: Regarding thematic fidelity and alignment results, they indicate a bounded, rather than general, thematic alignment between humans and synths.
The main problem was that the simulations retrieved only part of what appeared in the original groups and with different prevalence of each theme.

This pattern is consistent with the findings of Amirova et al. (2024), who found considerable correspondence in the main beliefs expressed by human and synthetic participants, along with much more pronounced differences in their structure and tone. Zhang et al. (2024) Profile enrichment improved this reconstruction, but not without a cost.
