text.text: The enriched agents recovered more of the human repertoire than agents grounded only in demographic information, supporting the broader finding that richer empirical grounding can improve behavioural prediction (Park et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The enriched agents recovered more of the human repertoire than agents grounded only in demographic information, supporting the broader finding that richer empirical grounding can improve behavioural prediction <ref type="bibr">(Park et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the themes that did emerge also spread across substantially more participants than in the human groups.
Enrichment therefore increased coverage while simultaneously concentrating the discussion around a narrower shared set of ideas.
This is particularly important because additional persona information is commonly assumed to increase individual differentiation.
Here, it did not simply make the agents "more human"; it changed which dimensions became collectively salient.

Although the present design cannot establish the mechanism, this pattern is compatible with the focalism described by Toubia et al. (2025), whereby explicitly supplied attributes become disproportionately influential in LLM-generated behaviour.
text.formatted: Although the present design cannot establish the mechanism, this pattern is compatible with the focalism described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Toubia et al. (2025)</ref>, whereby explicitly supplied attributes become disproportionately influential in LLM-generated behaviour.

text.text: The saturation results add a further consideration.
Neither synthetic condition reproduced the human trajectory, in which most themes emerged early, and the repertoire stabilised after the third group.
However, the two grounding approaches failed in different ways.
The basic condition showed a greater tendency towards premature saturation, in the most extreme case exhausting its entire thematic repertoire after the first group.

This reduces the marginal value of running additional focus groups as information can largely repeat, but in practice this is not a major problem since synthetic simulations are cheap and fast to run, unlike human fieldwork.
The enriched condition, by contrast, continued to introduce new themes across later sessions.

Although this accumulation was more uneven than the human pattern and did not converge at the same point, richer grounding appeared to preserve some thematic yield from conducting multiple groups rather than collapsing immediately onto a fixed repertoire.
Thus, enrichment did not reproduce human saturation, but it did make repeated synthetic sessions more informative.
The loss of themes or reduced prevalence of themes becomes particularly consequential when the purpose of the focus group is to capture the different facets of a phenomenon.
The case of gender illustrates this clearly.
At first glance, gender could appear to be a case of strong thematic fidelity: the idea that gender influences diet was among the most consistently reproduced themes in the synthetic groups.

However, within the human groups, this position coexisted with its categorical denial and with the position described in the original study as 'No influence, but…', namely participants who consciously rejected the relevance of gender while describing strongly gendered dietary practices.
The relationship between masculinity and diet therefore appeared, in some cases, to operate without a corresponding conscious articulation (Hankins et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The relationship between masculinity and diet therefore appeared, in some cases, to operate without a corresponding conscious articulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hankins et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The agents, on the other hand, tended to recognise and explicitly explain this relationship.

The fact that this pattern also appeared in the exclusively sociodemographic condition suggests that it cannot be explained entirely by the psychographic information provided to the enriched profiles.

One possible interpretation is that the model more readily reproduces available cultural knowledge about gender and diet than the resistance, contradiction or lack of awareness through which such knowledge may manifest itself in real individuals.

This resembles the 'hyper-accuracy distortion' identified by Amirova et al. (2024), whereby an LLM response can be well-informed, coherent and objectively plausible while remaining less faithful to the perspective it is intended to represent.
text.formatted: This resembles the 'hyper-accuracy distortion' identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amirova et al. (2024)</ref>, whereby an LLM response can be well-informed, coherent and objectively plausible while remaining less faithful to the perspective it is intended to represent.

text.text: In this case, the distortion can be understood as a form of interpretative overexplanation.
The agents verbalised a relationship that some human participants appeared to reproduce without directly recognising it.
The consequence is not simply that one position became more prevalent than another, but that part of the ambiguity surrounding the phenomenon was lost.
This suggests that fidelity may be particularly difficult to achieve when the topic involves social desirability, identity, resistance or a gap between behaviour and self-perception.
In such cases, a perfectly articulated response may in fact be less human.
Fidelity therefore depends not only on recovering the ideas present in a population, but also on preserving their contradictions, implicitness and uneven articulation.
The difference became clearer when the analysis shifted from content to interaction.
The synthetic turns were much longer, practically eliminated very short interventions, and showed considerably less direct continuity between participants than the human groups.

These patterns persisted even after a comparison of prompt versions that substantially reduced verbosity, suggesting that they cannot be attributed to an initial, poorly calibrated version of the prompt alone.
Importantly, the additional length did not translate into greater contextual richness.
Despite producing turns roughly five times longer at the median, both synthetic conditions contained fewer specific contextual references per 100 words than the human groups.
Enrichment improved this dimension relative to basic grounding alone, suggesting that additional participant information helped anchor responses in more relevant detail.

Yet it did not remove the broader interactional divergence: enriched and basic groups remained similarly verbose and displayed much less variation in conversational rhythm across sessions than humans.

Profile enrichment therefore appears more effective at changing what information agents draw upon their profiles as anchors than at changing the underlying discourse form through which that information is expressed.
Agents also frequently acknowledged a previous contribution, introduced an alternative position and then qualified or reconciled it within the same response.

This does not prove that there was either more consensus or more disagreement, but it does suggest that part of the deliberative process shifted from interaction between speakers to internal argumentation within the speaker.
In a human conversation, a position can be formulated briefly and left open for another person to contradict, reformulate or expand upon.
In the simulations, such alternative responses were more frequently anticipated by the agent themselves.
In this sense, they resembled, in some respects, the logic of a group interview, while still retaining characteristics specific to a multi-agent conversation.

This difference may help to explain why previous synthetic conversations have shown high levels of agreement. Mator et al. (2025), for example, found that synthetic responses were more extensive and showed considerably greater convergence than those of human participants.
text.formatted: This difference may help to explain why previous synthetic conversations have shown high levels of agreement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Mator et al. (2025)</ref>, for example, found that synthetic responses were more extensive and showed considerably greater convergence than those of human participants.

text.text: The current results suggest that some of this overlap may not be explained by complacency alone.
If several agents individually incorporate positions in favour, against and nuanced views, their responses will inevitably share more content, even if their final positions are not identical.
The apparent harmony may therefore arise partly from redundant discursive coverage, rather than from an interpersonal process of consensus-building.

Finally, synthetic participants were more linguistically similar to one another and substantially harder to identify or differentiate from each other using their responses, compared to human participants with no clear improvement from profile enrichment.
This suggests that providing agents with more individual information does not necessarily produce more individualised voices.

Persona construction therefore involves two challenges, generating responses that are plausible given a profile, and maintaining a recognisable individual who expresses and prioritises that information in a distinctive way.

An important methodological consideration is that these divergences were observed in a system that sought to structure the conditions of the focus group without directly prescribing its behavioural outcomes.

The architecture defined roles, conversational memory, participation mechanisms, access to the group context, moderation and progression through the guide, and explained to the agents what kind of interaction constituted a focus group.

However, apart from general adjustments designed to discourage overly rehearsed responses, no fixed response lengths, predetermined percentages of disagreement, turn-taking distributions, specific linguistic styles or participant-to-participant interaction quotas were imposed.
This was a deliberate decision.

Introducing these properties directly might have produced conversations that were superficially more human-like, but it would have incorporated into the system some of the very behaviours subsequently used to assess its fidelity.
For example, achieving turns of human-like length would be of little value as evidence if their length had been predetermined using the distribution observed in human transcripts.

Instead, the design sought to provide the necessary scaffolding for a focus group interaction to emerge, rather than hard-coding the behaviours against which that interaction would subsequently be assessed.

Under this logic, verbosity, the internalisation of contrast, or the reduced differentiation between voices are methodologically informative results precisely because they were not objectives programmed a priori.
This distinction also addresses the need for transparency in social simulation highlighted by Dilaver and Gilbert (2023), particularly when interpreting emergent properties of the model.
text.formatted: This distinction also addresses the need for transparency in social simulation highlighted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Dilaver and Gilbert (2023)</ref>, particularly when interpreting emergent properties of the model.

text.text: Reducing stylistic hard-coding was also intended to avoid an architecture that was overly dependent on the specific characteristics of a single LLM.

Different models may interpret very specific instructions regarding length, spontaneity or conversational style in different ways, therefore, exhaustively calibrating these characteristics for a specific model could reduce the system's portability or require re-engineering for each architecture.

This does not imply that the system has been shown to be modelindependent (something which this study did not evaluate), but rather that it was designed so that the greater part of the specification relates to the conditions of interaction rather than to a manual imitation of the linguistic and behavioural surface of the human reference.
These results support a usage-dependent assessment, rather than a binary classification of synthetic focus groups as valid or invalid.
For exploratory tasks, the advantages are significant.

The low cost, speed and ability to repeatedly run the same configuration make it possible to test guidelines, trial analytical procedures, identify candidate themes and explore scenarios before investing in human fieldwork.

The thematic accuracy observed suggests that these applications can produce plausible information, provided they are understood as exploratory input rather than a validated substitute for a human population.
However, the standard must be different when the question depends on relative salience, the presence of minority opinions, resistance or the collective construction of meaning.

Furthermore, the present results suggest that stability should be taken into account even within primarily thematic tasks: if a conclusion appears only in some runs, a single simulation does not allow us to determine whether a robust pattern or a favourable outcome has been identified.
In theoretical terms, the findings support the view that human-likeness should be understood as a multidimensional and situated property, rather than as a global attribute of a model.
Evaluating synthetic focus groups using a single similarity indicator may, therefore, obscure precisely the dimension whose reproduction is central to their intended use.
The current findings rely on a specific case: a particular population, a single topic, a single generative model and a specific architecture.
The results should not, therefore, be interpreted as universal properties of LLMs.
The three-level benchmark proposed here, however, is independent of the details of this case.

The benchmark allows us to assess the extent to which a textual, multi-agent architecture can approximate the observable functioning of a human focus group, even when the mechanisms governing conversation generation are not identical.

Beyond the performance of the simulations themselves, this study extends the emerging evidence on synthetic focus groups by evaluating their fidelity through several complementary dimensions within the same matched qualitative case.

Rather than reducing human-likeness to a single outcome, the benchmark examines thematic correspondence, interactional process, and agent-level fidelity, while repeated simulations allow the stability of apparent correspondence to be considered across runs.

Previous studies have provided important evidence on different aspects of synthetic focus-group performance; the present benchmark brings several of these concerns together within a common evaluative framework.
This makes it possible to examine not simply whether a simulation resembles its human reference, but which aspects are reproduced more closely, and which remain more difficult to approximate.

text.text: Conversely, the Basic synths, despite their overall lack of specificity, reach in two cases the lower bounds of the human range.
This suggests that the models generally struggle to naturally weave in the personal experiences and habits that ground human discourse in lived discussions.

The Enriched condition only outperforms the Basic one in the food-related category, likely because the explicit inclusion of dietary habits in their profiles provided the necessary cues for the model to generate those specific details.

text.text: Against this background of rapid, but unconsolidated progress, the general objective guiding this research aims to expand efforts to assess how reliably such systems can reproduce qualitative focus-group dynamics and, on that basis, how far their content approximates that of human groups in applied research settings.
Consequently, the next step is to examine how this technical progress has been structured and what specific results have been presented in this area.
thematic relevance of the content, the pattern of code saturation across sessions, and the interactional character of the discussion.
The first concerns whether the transcript covers the ideas and narratives needed to address the research objective.
The second concerns whether additional sessions generate new codes, and whether human and synthetic focus groups show a comparable point at which thematic novelty begins to decline.
The third concerns whether these themes emerge through recognisable group discussion.

The literature offers clearer guidance for saturation than for the other levels, since there is no standard expectation that focus groups should contain a fixed number of disagreements, peer responses, or challenges per question.

For this reason, the present study does not predefine what counts as a good discussion but uses the human transcripts as the reference point for comparison, asking whether synthetic groups reproduce similar patterns of discussion.
The indicators developed in the methodology are therefore intended as a pragmatic way to compare human and synthetic focus groups, rather than as general measures of focus group quality.
